title: First Job Memories: What Work Was Like in 1959

scenes.text: Do you remember your very first paycheck? Not the amount, maybe, but the feeling. The envelope with your name typed on it. The way you held it a little longer than you needed to before you opened it. For millions of Americans, that moment came in nineteen fifty-nine, and it felt like the whole world had just opened its doors.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST PAYCHECK

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-nine, a young person could walk into a factory, an office, a store or a diner, and walk out with a job the same afternoon. The country was growing fast. New highways, new suburbs, new supermarkets. Everything needed people to build it, run it, sell it and sweep up after it.
scenes.caption: HIRED THE SAME DAY

scenes.text: So let's go back. To the first job you ever had, the boss you never forgot, the uniform you had to wear, and the things that job taught you that no school ever could. These are first job memories, from nineteen fifty-nine.
scenes.caption: FIRST JOB MEMORIES

scenes.text: For a lot of us, work started long before the first real job. A paper route at eleven or twelve, with a canvas bag over your shoulder and fifty houses to reach before school. You folded every newspaper by hand, threw it onto the porch from your bicycle, and on Friday afternoons you went door to door to collect what each customer owed.
scenes.caption: THE PAPER ROUTE

scenes.text: You learned quickly who tipped and who didn't. Who paid right away, and who always said come back next week. That paper route taught a twelve-year-old more about money and people than any arithmetic book. And at Christmas, the good customers left an envelope with an extra quarter, or even a whole dollar.
scenes.caption: COLLECTION DAY

scenes.text: Girls babysat for the neighbors, for thirty-five or fifty cents an hour, and raided the refrigerator after the children were asleep. Boys mowed lawns with push mowers that had no engine at all, and shoveled snow off driveways in the winter. Every dollar went into a jar, or a passbook savings account at the bank downtown.
scenes.caption: FIFTY CENTS AN HOUR

scenes.text: And in the summer, there were the seasonal jobs. Picking strawberries or detasseling corn in the Midwest. Working the snack bar at the public pool. Bagging groceries at the supermarket, where the manager taught you to put the cans on the bottom and the bread on top, and to always say thank you, ma'am.
scenes.caption: SUMMER JOBS

scenes.text: Getting a real job in nineteen fifty-nine was simpler than it is now. You read the help wanted ads in the newspaper, which were divided into two columns, one for men and one for women. Or you heard about an opening from an uncle, a neighbor, or a friend at church. Then you put on your best clothes and went down in person.
scenes.caption: HELP WANTED

scenes.text: There was no computer and usually no resume. You filled out a one-page application in pen at a little desk in the personnel office. Then you sat across from a man in a suit, who asked where you went to school, what your father did, and whether you could start on Monday. Often, that was the whole interview.
scenes.caption: CAN YOU START MONDAY?

scenes.text: A handshake mattered. Looking a man in the eye mattered. Showing up on time, with your shoes shined and your hair combed, mattered more than almost anything you could write down on paper. Your father had told you so the night before, and for once, he was exactly right.
scenes.caption: A FIRM HANDSHAKE

scenes.text: Some jobs required a physical examination first, and some asked for a letter from your minister or your high school principal saying you were of good character. Girls applying for office work often took a typing test on the spot, in a back room, with a stopwatch ticking and a supervisor watching every keystroke.
scenes.caption: THE TYPING TEST

scenes.text: The first day was always the hardest. You didn't know where the lunchroom was, or the restroom, or which of the older workers you could trust. Somebody always played a joke on the new kid. Go ask the foreman for a left-handed wrench. Go find a bucket of steam. Everybody fell for it once.
scenes.caption: THE NEW KID

scenes.text: If you worked in a factory, you got a time card with your name on it, and you learned to punch the clock. In at seven. Lunch at eleven-thirty. Out at three-thirty. Be one minute late and the card showed it in red ink, and the foreman showed it on his face.
scenes.caption: PUNCHING THE CLOCK

scenes.text: If you worked in an office, you got a desk, a typewriter or an adding machine, and a stack of work by nine o'clock. The men wore white shirts and ties every single day. The women wore dresses, stockings and heels. And everybody, it seemed, smoked at their desks, so the whole office lived under a soft gray haze.
scenes.caption: WHITE SHIRTS AND TIES

scenes.text: If you worked in a store, you wore a uniform or a smock with your name sewn on it. You learned to make change in your head, counting it back into the customer's hand, starting from the price and working up to the bill they gave you. The cash register rang with a bell. There was no screen telling you what to give back.
scenes.caption: COUNTING BACK THE CHANGE

scenes.text: For a lot of young people, that first job was at a gas station, a diner, or a drive-in restaurant, where the carhops brought trays out to the cars and hooked them onto the half-open window. You ran all evening, smelled like french fries when you got home, and wouldn't have traded it for anything.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVE-IN

scenes.text: And if you worked on a farm, which was still the first job for millions of rural young people, there was no first day at all. You had been working since you were tall enough to carry a bucket. The difference now was that a neighbor paid you real wages to bale hay, milk cows, or drive a tractor through the long summer days.
scenes.caption: THE FARM

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-nine, the federal minimum wage was one dollar an hour. A factory job with a union might pay two dollars an hour or more. A young secretary might earn around fifty or sixty dollars a week. And for a teenager still living at home, even the smallest paycheck felt like a fortune.
scenes.caption: A DOLLAR AN HOUR

scenes.text: Many companies still paid in cash, in a small brown envelope, every Friday. Your name and the amount were written on the outside. Inside were the bills and coins, counted out by someone in the payroll office. You signed for it, slipped it into your pocket, and felt it there all the way home.
scenes.caption: THE BROWN ENVELOPE

scenes.text: And in a great many families, the first thing you did was give part of it to your mother. Room and board, they called it. Ten dollars a week, or whatever your parents asked. Nobody thought of it as unfair. You lived under their roof, you ate their food, and now you were helping, the way they had once helped their own parents.
scenes.caption: ROOM AND BOARD

scenes.text: With what was left, you bought things that felt like freedom. A transistor radio. A new pair of shoes. A record album for about three or four dollars. Saved up for a few months, it might become the down payment on a used car, which was the most important purchase a young person could make.
scenes.caption: WHAT YOU BOUGHT

scenes.text: A lot of young people also opened their first checking account that year, with a little book of checks that had their name printed in the corner. You wrote out your first check carefully, in your best handwriting, and then you worried about it for a week, until you were sure it hadn't bounced.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST CHECKBOOK

scenes.text: Taxes came out of your pay too, which surprised almost everybody. Federal income tax and Social Security. You stared at the stub and wondered who on earth FICA was, and why he was taking your money. Your father laughed and told you welcome to the club.
scenes.caption: WHO IS FICA?

scenes.text: Almost everybody had one. The boss who was tough but fair. Who yelled when you made a mistake, and then, a week later, quietly told the owner you were the best worker he'd hired in years. You may not have liked him then. But you probably still think about him now, more often than you'd expect.
scenes.caption: THE TOUGH BOSS

scenes.text: Or the older woman in the office who took you under her wing. Who showed you how to file, how to answer the phone, and how to handle the difficult customer without losing your temper. She'd been there twenty years. She knew where everything was, and everybody, even the boss, was a little afraid of her.
scenes.caption: THE WOMAN WHO KNEW EVERYTHING

scenes.text: Those people taught you things nobody writes down anymore. Show up early. Finish what you start. Take pride in work nobody will notice. Don't complain in front of the customers. Lessons like that stayed with you for fifty years, through every job that came after.
scenes.caption: WHAT THEY TAUGHT YOU

scenes.text: And then there were the friends you made. The other new hires who started the same week you did. You ate lunch together, covered for each other, went bowling on Thursday nights, and stood up at each other's weddings a few years later. Some of those friendships lasted the rest of your life.
scenes.caption: FRIENDS FROM WORK

scenes.text: Here's what may surprise younger people the most. In nineteen fifty-nine, a lot of people who took a first job at eighteen stayed with the same company for thirty or forty years. The company was loyal to them, and they were loyal to the company. When they retired, there was a dinner, a speech, and very often a gold watch.
scenes.caption: THE GOLD WATCH

scenes.text: There were company picnics in the summer, with three-legged races and a softball game between the office and the plant. There was a Christmas party, and a turkey or a ham for every family at Thanksgiving. The company newsletter printed your wedding, the birth of your children, and your bowling scores.
scenes.caption: THE COMPANY PICNIC

scenes.text: For the young men who were drafted, a first job often waited for them. The law protected their place, and many employers held the job open for two years while they served. Coming home in uniform and walking back through the same factory gate was a moment a lot of veterans of that era never forgot.
scenes.caption: THE JOB WAITED FOR YOU

scenes.text: It wasn't perfect. The work could be dull, hard and dangerous. Women were often paid far less than men for the same job, and many people were shut out of good jobs entirely because of the color of their skin. But for millions of families, a steady job meant a house, a car, and children who might someday go to college.
scenes.caption: NOT PERFECT

scenes.text: That first job was the moment you stopped being a child. Nobody gave you a certificate for it. There was no ceremony. But you came home one Friday with your own money in your pocket, and your father looked at you a little differently at the dinner table, and you knew something had changed.
scenes.caption: NO LONGER A CHILD

scenes.text: Maybe you still have a pay stub somewhere, or an old employee badge, or a photograph of yourself in that uniform, standing a little too straight. If you do, take it out tonight. Look at that young face. That person had no idea what was coming. But they were ready to work for it.
scenes.caption: THAT YOUNG FACE

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was your very first job, and how much did it pay? We read every one of them. And stay with us, because next we're going to look at what a whole paycheck really bought in nineteen sixty-two. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR FIRST JOB?
